opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, hands are still one of the hardest parts, and I try to be candid about that.

When someone asks for a humanoid with dexterous hands, I look at it on a few levels. First is the basic topology: are there five distinct fingers, is the thumb opposable and placed correctly, are the fingers fused together into a sort of mitten? A lot of generative 3D models, especially earlier ones, would give you something that looks fine in a thumbnail but falls apart up close: the fingers merge, or you get a webbed blob.

Second is whether it's actually usable downstream. For a game developer or an animator, a hand isn't just something to look at. It needs to be riggable. So I'm asking: is there enough geometry around the knuckles so it can bend? Are the fingers separated enough that auto-rigging can put bones in them? If the mesh is clean but the fingers are glued together, it's not really a dexterous hand. It's a sculpture of one.

Third is texture and consistency. Sometimes the geometry is okay, but the texture paints in finger lines that don't match the actual shape, so it looks right from the front and wrong from the side. That's a classic multi-view inconsistency issue.

So my honest assessment is that we've made big progress. Hands went from basically unusable to often acceptable. But for truly dexterous, production-ready hands, I'd still say it's an active area. Fine, small, articulated structures are exactly where the resolution and the 3D priors of these models get stressed. Internally we treat hands, faces, and thin structures as the stress tests. If your model can do hands well, it's probably doing a lot of other things right too.

r001.rationale: The response says dexterous, production-ready hands remain an active challenge and discusses rigging and articulated structures, but it does not clearly state that the AI-generated hand lacks articulation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is actually one of my favorite test cases, because hands are where most of these systems fall apart, and they fall apart in ways that are very easy to miss if you only look at a rendered turntable.

So when we get a humanoid back with "dexterous hands" in the prompt, the first thing I do is ignore the beauty render and look at the mesh topology around the fingers. A lot of generative pipelines will give you something that looks like five fingers from three feet away, but when you zoom in, fingers are fused at the base, the webbing is a blob, or two fingers share geometry. If the mesh isn't actually five separate, cleanly separated digits with reasonable edge loops at the knuckles, it's not dexterous, it's a sculpture of a hand. And that distinction matters a lot for us because we care about simulation, not just display.

The second thing is proportions and joint placement. Humans are extremely sensitive to hands. The thumb is almost always the problem. Models will put the thumb in the wrong plane, or make it the same length as the index finger, or give it the wrong number of segments. I'll literally count phalanges. Four fingers with three segments each, thumb with two, and the thumb's base joint needs to be opposable, meaning it rotates on a different axis than the other fingers. If that's wrong, nothing downstream can fix it.

Then, if the asset is supposed to be rigged, I check whether the joint hierarchy makes physical sense. Can the fingers actually curl without the skin collapsing? Does the palm deform or stay rigid? Does the knuckle bend in the right direction? A surprising number of "rigged" outputs have bones that are inside the mesh but not aligned with where the real joints would be, so the moment you pose it, the geometry tears or the fingers bend sideways.

And honestly, the deeper test for me is functional: can this hand grasp something? If I drop a simple object, a cup or a sphere, into a physics scene and try to close the fingers around it, do I get plausible contact? Does it self-intersect? That's the real bar for "dexterous." The word implies capability, not appearance.

So my grading is roughly in that order: topology, anatomy, rig correctness, then functional behavior under simulation. Most AI-generated hands today pass the first glance and fail by step two or three. The ones that get all four are still pretty rare, and when we see them it's usually because the pipeline had some explicit structural prior for hands rather than treating the whole body as one undifferentiated mesh.

r001.rationale: The response describes topology, joint-placement, and rigging problems that can prevent proper movement, but it does not state that the AI-generated hand lacks articulation.

astra-6.text: I’d look beyond whether it resembles a hand. Are the fingers distinct, are the joints placed sensibly, and can the thumb oppose the fingers? Then I’d check whether the hand can actually be articulated to grasp and manipulate objects. A hand that looks convincing in a static image doesn’t necessarily satisfy a request for dexterous hands. Without seeing the generated asset or testing its movement, I couldn’t say whether this particular hand meets that requirement.

sol-6.1.text: I’d look at whether the hand is actually usable, beyond whether it looks convincing. Are the fingers and joints structured correctly? Can they move independently, and does the mesh deform properly when the hand closes or grasps an object? If the request is for dexterous hands, a good-looking static hand isn’t enough. You need to test the articulation and see whether it supports the motions you need.
